# Concepts

This chapter outlines several concepts that are encountered within statistics
applied to clinical trials.

## Objectives

A clinical trial must have a primary objective (aim), and can have one or more
secondary objectives.

### Safety

For each new treatment, investigators must assess whether it is **acceptable**
and **safe** for use, and check what side effects it may cause. When focusing on
safety, the investigators focus on the occurrence of adverse events (AE),
serious adverse events (SAE), abnormal laboratory findings, tolerability issues,
etc.

The main questions are:

* Is the treatment acceptable for use in humans?
* Is the treatment safe for use in humans?
* Does the treatment cause any side effects?

### Efficacy

For each new treatment, the investigators must assess if the treatment actually
helps with the issue at hand. The treatment must alleviate symptoms or provide a
cure in order for it to be considered to have an effect. Efficacy focuses on the
effect of the treatment **under ideal conditions**, i.e., in a strongly
regulated environment, such as a clinical trial where patients are followed up
on closely.

To estimate efficacy of a treatment, the **per-protocol set** (PPS) of patients
must be analyzed. In the case of intercurrent events, the hypothetical strategy
assists in finding an estimate for the efficacy.

The main questions are:

* Does the treatment actually work in ideal conditions?
* How well does the treatment perform in ideal conditions?

### Effectiveness

Effectiveness seems the same as efficacy, but it focuses on the real-world
effect of the treatment. Under ideal conditions, investigators can assess
whether the treatment has any potential of an effect. In the real world,
however, an initiated treatment may be stopped, or patients have to take rescue
medication. The questions remains, then, if the treatment still performs as
well.

To estimate effectiveness of a treatment, the **full analysis set** (FAS)
(intention to treat (ITT) set) of patients must be analyzed. In the case of
intercurrent events, the treatment policy strategy assts in assessing
effectiveness.

The main questions are:

* Does the treatment actually work in real-world conditions?
* How well does the treatment perform in real-world conditions?

### Usability

A treatment must also be usable for the users. Users include patients but also
caregivers and clinicians.

## Definitions

### Endpoints

An endpoint is a patient-level quantity for which there is one value per
patient. It can be derived from a single observation or measurement per patient,
or it can be a composite endpoint. An example can be the occurrence of a
cardiovascular event, which is defined as the occurrence of a stroke, a
myocardial infarction, or another cardiovascular event.
